books.section: Unit 5: Toward the Civil War and Reconstruction (1844–1877)

stimulus.source_note: Map of the United States, the Area of Freedom and Slavery, published by G. W. Elliott, New York, 1856; public domain.
stimulus.text: A wall map printed in New York in 1856 is titled “Map of the United States, the Area of Freedom and Slavery, and the Territories Whose Destiny Is Yet to Be Decided.” It colors the free states pink and the slave states gray, draws the Missouri Compromise line at 36°30′ across the West, and shows portraits of John C. Frémont (left) and William L. Dayton (right) at the top. Below the map, tables compare the free states and the slave states using figures from the United States census of 1850.

source: original; stimulus image from the shared pool, Map of the United States, the Area of Freedom and Slavery (1856), public domain
stem: The map was printed in 1856, the year Frémont and Dayton ran for president and vice president on the new Republican ticket. The portraits and the census tables were most likely included to

options.text: prove that the South had more people, more wealth, and more land than the North.
options.misconception: The tables were printed to show the free states ahead, not the slave states.

options.text: persuade voters that free states were stronger and more prosperous than slave states, and that slavery should not spread.
warn voters that Frémont planned to abolish slavery in the Southern states at once, by force if needed.
options.misconception: The Republican platform of 1856 opposed slavery’s extension, not immediate abolition in the South.

options.text: show that the Missouri Compromise line had settled the slavery question for good and for all time.
options.misconception: The line had been repealed in 1854, which is why the territories were “yet to be decided.”

rationales.A: A Republican campaign map would not print tables proving the slave states stronger.
rationales.B: The portraits tie the map to the Republican candidates, and the tables use census figures to compare the free and slave states side by side. Background from the books: the Republican Party organized in 1854 against slavery’s expansion, and its free-soil case was that free labor built stronger states than slave labor.
rationales.C: Frémont ran on keeping slavery out of the territories, not on abolishing it where it already existed.
rationales.D: The map calls the territories undecided, so its makers thought the line had failed, not settled the question.
rationales.general:
1. Note who is pictured. Frémont and Dayton, the 1856 Republican candidates, sit at the top of the map.
2. Note what is printed below. Tables from the 1850 census compare the free states and the slave states side by side.
3. Ask what the makers wanted voters to conclude. The free states look stronger and more prosperous, so slavery should not spread.
4. Name the purpose. This is a campaign document arguing the free-soil case with numbers.
Remember: when a source prints statistics beside candidates’ portraits, the numbers are part of the pitch.
